summary.text: Sea surface temperature is the temperature of ocean water near the surface, usually measured somewhere between 1 millimetre and 20 metres down.
It shapes the air above it: warm surface water can build and strengthen cyclones, and coastal values help forecasters predict sea breezes and sea fog.
Global mean sea surface temperature very likely rose by 0.88 °C between 1850–1900 and 2011–2020 because of global warming.

facts.label: Depth meant by surface
facts.value: Usually between 1 mm and 20 m down

facts.label: Daily swing
facts.value: Can vary by 6 °C on calm days

items.prompt: A hurricane has just crossed a stretch of warm tropical sea. What happens to the water temperature along its track?

options.label: It warms from the storm's heat
It stays exactly the same
It cools as the storm stirs the water
It warms because rain is warm

items.explain: Tropical cyclones leave a cool wake because they churn up and mix the top 30 metres of the ocean.

items.prompt: You log the sea temperature at a beach every hour for two days, one calm and one breezy. Which day shows the bigger swing?

options.label: The calm day
The breezy day
Both swing the same
Neither swings at all

items.explain: Sea surface temperature varies less on breezy days than on calm days, when it can shift by as much as 6 °C.

items.prompt: Over a sunny day the sea surface warms and cools much less than the air above it. Why?

options.label: Salt blocks most of the sunlight
The sea is always moving faster
Cold rivers keep pouring into it
Water has greater thermal inertia

items.explain: The sea surface has a daily temperature range like the air, but smaller, because of its greater thermal inertia.

items.prompt: Along a coast, winds push the sun-warmed top layer of the sea out away from shore. What happens to the water near the beach?

options.label: It gets warmer as it piles up
Cooler water rises from below
It drains away and sea level drops
It freezes into a thin crust

items.explain: When winds move warm surface water offshore, cooler water from below replaces it, a process called Ekman transport.

items.prompt: Off a large river delta, fresh river water spreads over the top of the salty sea. How does that top layer warm in the sun?

options.label: Slower, since fresh water holds less heat
Exactly as fast as open ocean
Faster, since it mixes little with below
It cannot warm until it turns salty

items.explain: Freshwater floats over the denser seawater, and with little vertical mixing it heats faster.

items.prompt: What can a patch of unusually warm sea surface do to a storm passing over it?

options.label: Help it grow stronger
Break it up quickly
Turn its rain into snow
Stop it from moving

items.explain: Warm sea surface temperatures can develop and strengthen cyclones over the ocean.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as the surface
paragraphs.text: Sea surface temperature is how warm the ocean is near its top. What counts as the surface depends on how it is measured, but it lies somewhere between 1 millimetre and 20 metres down. The very top film, about 20 micrometres thick, has its own name: the skin temperature. Water below the surface layer is described by ocean temperature, or deeper ocean temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Why there is no single depth
paragraphs.text: How far the surface layer reaches depends on how much it mixes with the water beneath. In the tropics a warm top layer of about 100 m stays stable and barely mixes downward. Near the poles, winter cold and storms make the top water denser, so it mixes very deep before layering again in summer. So there is no one simple depth for the ocean surface. The ocean's photic depth, typically about 100 m and up to around 200 m in the open ocean, is tied to this heated layer.

paragraphs.heading: Daily ups and downs
paragraphs.text: Like the air, the sea surface warms and cools over a day, but by less. The sea has greater thermal inertia, so its swing is smaller. Even so, the surface can change by 6 °C on a calm day, while breezy days bring smaller changes. Deeper water follows the air with a delay of 15 days for every 10 metres. In the Aral Sea this means the water near the bottom is warmest in December and coldest in May and June.

paragraphs.heading: Shaping weather and storms
paragraphs.text: Sea surface temperature changes the air above it, especially air masses close to the shore. Forecasting models use coastal values because they help produce sea breezes and sea fog. Warm surface water can help cyclones form and grow stronger over the ocean. A tropical cyclone can also leave a cool wake behind it, as it churns the top 30 metres of water. Satellites can spot this cooling, which comes mainly from a deepening mixed layer and heat lost from the surface.

paragraphs.heading: Coasts, rivers and dust
paragraphs.text: Near some coasts, winds push warm surface water out to sea and cooler water rises from below to take its place, a process called Ekman transport. This usually brings more nutrients for sea life. Off river deltas, fresh water spreads over the heavier seawater and warms faster because it mixes little with the water below. After Saharan dust storms lasting several days, the nearby northern Atlantic surface cools by 0.2 C to 0.4 C. Storms outside the tropics, sudden floods of glacial meltwater and dense blooms of phytoplankton can also cause short-lived changes.

paragraphs.heading: A warming surface
paragraphs.text: Global warming has very likely lifted the average sea surface temperature worldwide by 0.88 °C, comparing 1850–1900 with 2011–2020. Most of that, 0.60 °C, came between 1980 and 2020. Land is warming faster than the sea, because the ocean takes in about 90% of the excess heat from climate change. Since 1950 the tropical ocean has warmed fastest, especially the tropical Indian Ocean, the western Pacific and the western boundary currents of the subtropical gyres. The eastern Pacific, the subtropical North Atlantic and the Southern Ocean have warmed more slowly than average, or even cooled.

paragraphs.heading: Swings over decades
paragraphs.text: Some changes play out over decades. The Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, or AMO, is a major driver of North Atlantic surface temperatures and Northern Hemisphere climate. What controls it is still poorly understood: the atmosphere's own variability, shifts in ocean circulation or human influence may all play a part. North Atlantic changes may even alter winds over the subtropical North Pacific and warm the western Pacific. El Niño, in turn, is defined by long-lasting departures of Pacific surface temperatures from their average.
